items.meaning: Used to transition from one topic to the next in a presentation or discussion.
items.example: Now that we've covered the budget, let's move on to the project timeline.
items.plain: Now that we've covered the budget, we will discuss the project timeline next.
items.note: Very common and natural way to change topics. Suitable for most professional settings.

items.meaning: Used to introduce the starting point or initial focus of your talk.
items.example: I'd like to begin by thanking you all for coming today.
items.plain: I want to start by thanking everyone for attending today.
items.note: A polite and standard opening for a presentation. Slightly formal but widely used.

items.meaning: Used to quickly summarise the main points that have just been discussed.
items.example: To recap briefly, we've discussed the market trends and our current strategy.
items.plain: To quickly summarise, we've talked about market trends and our current strategy.
items.note: Useful for reinforcing information or reminding the audience of previous points.

items.meaning: Used to signal the end of your presentation and introduce your final thoughts.
items.example: In conclusion, I'd like to reiterate the importance of teamwork.
items.plain: To finish, I want to repeat that teamwork is very important.
items.note: A classic and clear way to end a presentation. Very formal and professional.

items.text: What I want to focus on now
items.form: What I want to focus on now
items.meaning: Used to direct the audience's attention to the specific topic you will discuss next.
items.example: What I want to focus on now is the impact of these changes on our customers.
items.plain: Now, I will discuss the impact of these changes on our customers.
items.note: A direct and clear way to introduce a new section or emphasize a particular point.

items.meaning: Used to show how the previous point naturally leads into the next one.
items.example: The success of the pilot project this brings me to our expansion plans.
items.plain: The success of the pilot project leads us to our expansion plans.
items.note: Creates a smooth transition between related ideas. Sounds very natural.

items.meaning: Used to draw attention to information that is visible, often on a slide or chart.
items.example: As you can see from the graph, sales have increased significantly.
items.plain: The graph shows that sales have increased significantly.
items.note: Common when referring to visual aids. Can be used to highlight obvious points.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a general summary or outline of what will be covered.
items.example: To give you an overview, I'll discuss three key areas today.
items.plain: I will provide a general summary of the three key areas today.
items.note: A good way to set expectations at the beginning of a talk. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize the most important point or the first thing to consider.
items.example: First and foremost, we need to address the security concerns.
items.plain: Most importantly, we need to address the security concerns.
items.note: Adds emphasis to a primary point. Sounds quite formal and assertive.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a contrasting point or a qualification to what was just stated.
items.example: The project is challenging; having said that, I'm confident in our team.
items.plain: The project is challenging; however, I'm confident in our team.
items.note: A useful phrase for showing balance or acknowledging a counter-argument.

items.meaning: Used to offer more details or a fuller explanation of a previous point.
items.example: Let me elaborate on the reasons behind our decision to change suppliers.
items.plain: I will provide more details about why we decided to change suppliers.
items.note: Polite and professional way to expand on an idea. Often used in Q&A.

items.meaning: Used to rephrase something in simpler or clearer terms.
items.example: Our goal is to streamline operations; to put it another way, we want to work smarter.
items.plain: Our goal is to streamline operations; we want to work smarter.
items.note: Helpful for ensuring clarity, especially when explaining complex ideas.

items.meaning: Used to explain something more simply or differently, often after a complex statement.
items.example: The data suggests a paradigm shift; in other words, a fundamental change is occurring.
items.plain: The data suggests a fundamental change is occurring.
items.note: Very common for clarification. Can be used to simplify jargon.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a brief statement of the main points of a discussion or presentation.
items.example: To summarise, our strategy focuses on innovation and customer satisfaction.
items.plain: Our strategy focuses on innovation and customer satisfaction.
items.note: A standard way to conclude a section or the entire talk. Formal.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you will cover a series of points rapidly.
items.example: I'll just quickly run through the agenda for today's meeting.
items.plain: I will quickly go over the agenda for today's meeting.
items.note: Suggests efficiency and brevity. Common in informal professional settings.

items.meaning: Used to indicate the next topic or section that will be discussed.
items.example: First, we'll review the results, and we'll then look at the next steps.
items.plain: First, we'll review the results, and next we will discuss the next steps.
items.note: A straightforward way to signpost the flow of your presentation.

items.meaning: Used to introduce the last point you will discuss, often briefly.
items.example: Finally, I'll touch on the potential risks associated with this approach.
items.plain: Lastly, I will briefly mention the potential risks of this approach.
items.note: Signals the approaching end of a section or the presentation. Polite.

items.meaning: Used to pause and check for understanding or invite questions before continuing.
items.example: Before I go on, are there any questions about the previous section?
items.plain: Are there any questions about the previous section before I continue?
items.note: A natural way to create an interactive moment during a presentation.

items.meaning: Used to indicate a shift in focus to future actions, plans, or developments.
items.example: Moving forward, we plan to implement these changes by the end of the quarter.
items.plain: In the future, we plan to implement these changes by the end of the quarter.
items.note: Common in business contexts to discuss next steps or future strategy.

items.meaning: Used to invite the audience to think about a particular idea or aspect.
items.example: Let's consider the implications of these findings for our long-term strategy.
items.plain: We should think about the implications of these findings for our long-term strategy.
items.note: Engages the audience and encourages reflection. Professional and inclusive.

items.text: I'd like to draw your attention to
items.form: I'd like to draw your attention to
items.meaning: Used to politely ask the audience to focus on a specific detail or point.
items.example: I'd like to draw your attention to the third bullet point on the slide.
items.plain: Please look at the third bullet point on the slide.
items.note: A formal and polite way to highlight something important. Very professional.

items.meaning: Used to show a logical progression from one idea or result to the next.
items.example: The positive feedback from users this leads us to our next product iteration.
items.plain: The positive feedback from users means we will now work on our next product iteration.
items.note: Similar to 'This brings me to', but often implies a consequence or next step.

items.meaning: Used to introduce an example or anecdote that clarifies a previous statement.
items.example: To illustrate this point, let me share a brief case study.
items.plain: Let me share a brief case study to explain this idea.
items.note: Common before providing evidence or an example. Professional and clear.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a specific instance that demonstrates a general statement.
items.example: Many companies are adopting this, for example, our main competitor.
items.plain: Many companies are adopting this, including our main competitor.
items.note: A fundamental phrase for providing evidence or clarification. Very common.

items.meaning: Used to highlight one specific item or aspect among several.
items.example: We've seen growth in several areas, in particular, our online sales.
items.plain: We've seen growth in several areas, especially our online sales.
items.note: Adds emphasis to a specific detail. Can be used to narrow focus.

items.meaning: Used to introduce the consequence or outcome of a previous action or event.
items.example: We implemented new software, and as a result, efficiency improved.
items.plain: We implemented new software, and efficiency improved because of it.
items.note: Clearly links cause and effect. Very common in explanations and reports.

items.meaning: Used to provide a concise summary or the main point of something.
items.example: The project faced many hurdles; in short, it was a difficult year.
items.plain: The project faced many hurdles; it was a difficult year.
items.note: Good for brevity and getting straight to the point. Can be used informally too.

items.meaning: Used to signal the end of a presentation or a section and introduce final remarks.
items.example: To conclude, I believe we are well-positioned for future growth.
items.plain: Finally, I believe we are well-positioned for future growth.
items.note: A formal and standard way to end a talk. Similar to 'In conclusion'.

items.meaning: Used to introduce the first point or the starting consideration of a discussion.
items.example: To begin with, let's review the current market conditions.
items.plain: First, let's review the current market conditions.
items.note: A common and natural way to start a discussion or list of points.

items.meaning: Used to informally introduce the next item on an agenda or the next speaker.
items.example: Next up, we have Sarah to talk about the marketing campaign.
items.plain: Sarah will speak next about the marketing campaign.
items.note: More informal than 'Next, we will look at'. Suitable for team meetings.

items.meaning: Used to clarify or rephrase something you've just said, often to make it clearer.
items.example: It's a complex issue; what I mean is, there's no simple solution.
items.plain: It's a complex issue; there's no simple solution.
items.note: Very common in spoken English for clarification. Can be used to simplify.

items.meaning: The most important piece of information or conclusion to remember from a presentation.
items.example: For me, the main takeaway from this report is the need for immediate action.
items.plain: For me, the most important conclusion from this report is the need for immediate action.
items.note: A popular phrase in business to refer to the core message. Informal but widely accepted.

items.meaning: The most important results or discoveries from research or analysis.
items.example: Let's now discuss the key findings of our recent customer survey.
items.plain: Let's now discuss the most important results of our recent customer survey.
items.note: Standard academic and business terminology. Professional and clear.

items.meaning: A very important part or feature of something.
items.example: The budget is a crucial aspect of any project planning process.
items.plain: The budget is a very important part of any project planning process.
items.note: Emphasizes the significance of a particular element. Formal.

items.meaning: A fundamental or absolutely necessary idea or piece of information.
items.example: The essential point here is that we must adapt to market changes.
items.plain: The most important idea here is that we must adapt to market changes.
items.note: Highlights a core idea that cannot be overlooked. Professional.

items.meaning: The central or most important idea that someone is trying to communicate.
items.example: The core message of my presentation is about sustainable growth.
items.plain: The main idea of my presentation is about sustainable growth.
items.note: Refers to the central theme or purpose. Common in communication and marketing.

items.meaning: Used to invite the audience to ask questions about what has been presented up to that point.
items.example: I've covered a lot of ground; any questions so far?
items.plain: I've covered a lot of ground; do you have any questions?
items.note: A very common and natural way to check for understanding during a talk.

items.meaning: Used to politely offer to provide a response to a question.
items.example: That's a great point, and I'd be happy to answer that for you.
items.plain: That's a great point, and I can answer that for you.
items.note: A polite and welcoming way to respond to a question. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to encourage the audience to ask questions at any time during the presentation.
items.example: If anything is unclear, please feel free to interrupt with your questions.
items.plain: If anything is unclear, please ask your questions at any time.
items.note: Creates a more interactive and less formal atmosphere. Common in workshops.

items.meaning: Used to acknowledge the value or relevance of a question asked by an audience member.
items.example: That's a good question, and it touches on a key challenge.
items.plain: That's a relevant question, and it touches on a key challenge.
items.note: A polite way to buy a moment to think and validate the questioner.

items.meaning: Used to defer answering a question because it will be covered in a subsequent section.
items.example: That's an excellent point, and I'll get to that later in my presentation.
items.plain: That's an excellent point, and I will discuss that later in my presentation.
items.note: A polite way to manage the flow of information without dismissing the question.

items.meaning: Used to offer a clearer or more precise explanation of something previously said.
items.example: Let me clarify what I meant by 'strategic alignment' in this context.
items.plain: I will explain more clearly what I meant by 'strategic alignment' in this context.
items.note: Very useful when you sense confusion or need to be more exact. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to politely ask someone to provide more details or explanation about their point.
items.example: That's an interesting idea; could you elaborate on that a little more?
items.plain: That's an interesting idea; could you explain that in more detail?
items.note: A polite way to seek more information from a questioner or another speaker.

items.meaning: Used to directly address a question that has been asked.
items.example: To answer your question, yes, we have considered alternative solutions.
items.plain: Yes, we have considered alternative solutions.
items.note: A clear and direct way to begin your response to a query. Professional.

items.text: I hope that answers your question
items.form: I hope that answers your question
items.meaning: Used to politely conclude your response and check if the questioner is satisfied.
items.example: I've explained the process in detail, so I hope that answers your question.
items.plain: I've explained the process in detail, so I hope you are satisfied with the answer.
items.note: A polite closing to a Q&A interaction. Professional and considerate.

items.text: Perhaps we can discuss that offline
items.form: Perhaps we can discuss that offline
items.meaning: Used to suggest continuing a detailed or specific discussion privately after the presentation.
items.example: That's a very specific technical query; perhaps we can discuss that offline.
items.plain: That's a very specific technical query; maybe we can talk about it after the presentation.
items.note: Useful for managing time or when a question is too niche for the whole audience.

items.text: I'm afraid I don't have that information
items.form: I'm afraid I don't have that information
items.meaning: Used to politely state that you do not possess the requested data or knowledge.
items.example: I'm afraid I don't have that information readily available right now.
items.plain: I don't have that information available right now.
items.note: A polite and professional way to admit you don't know something. Avoids guessing.

items.text: That's outside the scope of this presentation
items.form: That's outside the scope of this presentation
items.meaning: Used to indicate that a question is not relevant to the current topic being discussed.
items.example: While interesting, that's outside the scope of this presentation.
items.plain: While interesting, that topic is not part of this presentation.
items.note: A polite but firm way to keep the discussion focused. Professional.

items.text: We'll have time for questions at the end
items.form: We'll have time for questions at the end
items.meaning: Used to inform the audience that a dedicated Q&A session will occur later.
items.example: Please hold your thoughts; we'll have time for questions at the end.
items.plain: Please hold your thoughts; we will answer questions at the end.
items.note: A standard way to manage audience interaction and maintain presentation flow.

items.meaning: Used to signal that you are about to conclude the Q&A session.
items.example: We're running short on time, so I'll take one more question.
items.plain: We're running short on time, so I will answer one more question.
items.note: A clear way to manage time and wrap up the Q&A. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to express gratitude to an audience member for asking a question.
items.example: Thank you for your question; it's an important point to consider.
items.plain: Your question is an important point to consider.
items.note: A polite and standard opening to an answer, showing appreciation.

items.meaning: Used to ensure that a statement or explanation is fully understood and unambiguous.
items.example: Just to be clear, our target market is young professionals, not students.
items.plain: To be clear, our target market is young professionals, not students.
items.note: Very common for ensuring precision and avoiding misunderstandings. Natural.

items.meaning: Used to rephrase or clarify a previous statement that might have been misunderstood.
items.example: I said 'challenging', but what I meant was 'requiring careful planning'.
items.plain: I said 'challenging', but I meant 'requiring careful planning'.
items.note: Useful for correcting a slip or providing a more accurate explanation.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you will express something again in different words for clarity.
items.example: My apologies, let me rephrase that to make it more precise.
items.plain: My apologies, I will say that again in a more precise way.
items.note: A polite way to correct oneself or improve clarity. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to politely indicate that you don't understand what someone is saying.
items.example: I'm not sure I follow your reasoning on that last point.
items.plain: I don't understand your reasoning on that last point.
items.note: A polite and common way to ask for clarification without sounding rude.

items.meaning: Used to politely ask someone to say something again, often because you didn't hear or understand.
items.example: I missed the last part; could you repeat that, please?
items.plain: I missed the last part; please say that again.
items.note: A standard and polite request for repetition. Very common.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you have grasped the meaning, possibly with a slight reservation.
items.example: Okay, I think I understand your perspective on the budget constraints.
items.plain: Okay, I understand your perspective on the budget constraints.
items.note: A cautious way to confirm understanding, leaving room for further clarification.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a simplified explanation of a complex idea.
items.example: The algorithm optimizes resource allocation; to put it simply, it makes things more efficient.
items.plain: The algorithm optimizes resource allocation; it makes things more efficient.
items.note: Excellent for breaking down complex information for a general audience.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize a particular piece of information that the audience should remember.
items.example: It's important to note that these figures are projections, not actuals.
items.plain: Remember that these figures are projections, not actuals.
items.note: A very common and effective way to highlight key information. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to draw attention to the most vital element or aspect of a situation.
items.example: What's crucial here is our ability to adapt quickly to market changes.
items.plain: Our ability to adapt quickly to market changes is the most important thing here.
items.note: Adds strong emphasis to a critical point. Sounds assertive.

items.meaning: Used to strongly emphasize a particular point or statement.
items.example: I want to stress that collaboration is essential for this project's success.
items.plain: Collaboration is essential for this project's success.
items.note: A direct and forceful way to highlight importance. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to remind the audience of an important fact or consideration.
items.example: Bear in mind that the timeline is ambitious, but achievable.
items.plain: Remember that the timeline is ambitious, but achievable.
items.note: A common way to introduce a caveat or an important piece of context.

items.meaning: Used to remind the audience of an important fact or consideration.
items.example: Keep in mind that our competitors are also innovating rapidly.
items.plain: Remember that our competitors are also innovating rapidly.
items.note: Interchangeable with 'Bear in mind that'. Very common and natural.

items.meaning: Used to state that a particular point or factor is extremely important.
items.example: Understanding customer needs, this is key to developing successful products.
items.plain: Understanding customer needs is extremely important for developing successful products.
items.note: A concise and impactful way to emphasize significance. Direct.

items.meaning: Especially significant or noteworthy among other important things.
items.example: The feedback from early adopters is of particular importance to us.
items.plain: The feedback from early adopters is especially important to us.
items.note: A formal way to highlight something as being more important than others.

items.meaning: Used to state the most significant idea or argument being made.
items.example: The main point is that we need to prioritize long-term sustainability.
items.plain: We need to prioritize long-term sustainability.
items.note: A clear way to summarize or emphasize the core message. Very common.

items.meaning: Used to suggest that a specific piece of information is valuable to keep in mind.
items.example: It's worth remembering that market conditions can change rapidly.
items.plain: Remember that market conditions can change rapidly.
items.note: A gentle but firm way to highlight an important consideration. Professional.

items.text: I cannot overstate the importance of
items.form: I cannot overstate the importance of
items.meaning: Used to strongly emphasize that something is extremely important.
items.example: I cannot overstate the importance of clear communication in a remote team.
items.plain: Clear communication is extremely important in a remote team.
items.note: A very strong way to emphasize something. Sounds formal and serious.

items.meaning: Used to state that something is absolutely necessary or fundamental.
items.example: It's essential to conduct thorough market research before launching.
items.plain: It is absolutely necessary to conduct thorough market research before launching.
items.note: A strong way to convey necessity. Professional and direct.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that something is more important than anything else.
items.example: Above all, we must maintain our commitment to quality.
items.plain: Most importantly, we must maintain our commitment to quality.
items.note: Adds strong emphasis to the paramount consideration. Formal.

items.meaning: Used to express certainty or strong conviction about a statement.
items.example: Without a doubt, this is our most ambitious project to date.
items.plain: This is certainly our most ambitious project to date.
items.note: A strong expression of certainty. Can be used in both formal and informal contexts.

items.meaning: Used to state that something is so obvious that it doesn't need to be mentioned.
items.example: It goes without saying that data privacy is paramount in our work.
items.plain: Data privacy is obviously paramount in our work.
items.note: Often used to state a fundamental truth or a widely accepted principle.

items.meaning: Used to introduce the most important fact or the essential truth of a situation.
items.example: We can discuss details, but the bottom line is we need to increase sales.
items.plain: We can discuss details, but the most important thing is we need to increase sales.
items.note: A common phrase in business to get to the core issue. Slightly informal.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that evidence or data unequivocally supports a conclusion.
items.example: The survey results this clearly shows a preference for flexible working.
items.plain: The survey results clearly demonstrate a preference for flexible working.
items.note: Strongly links evidence to a conclusion. Professional and assertive.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize that something is absolutely necessary for success or survival.
items.example: It's vital that we secure additional funding for the next phase.
items.plain: It is absolutely necessary that we secure additional funding for the next phase.
items.note: A very strong way to express necessity. More emphatic than 'important'.

items.text: What I meant to say was
items.form: What I meant to say was
items.meaning: Used to correct a previous statement and provide the intended meaning.
items.example: Apologies, what I meant to say was that the deadline is Friday, not Thursday.
items.plain: Apologies, the deadline is Friday, not Thursday.
items.note: A very common and natural way to correct a verbal slip. Polite.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are about to fix an error in your previous statement.
items.example: Actually, let me correct myself; the figures are from last quarter, not this one.
items.plain: Actually, the figures are from last quarter, not this one.
items.note: A direct and clear way to acknowledge and fix an error. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to correct or refine a previous statement, offering a more accurate term.
items.example: We're targeting a new demographic, or rather, expanding into an adjacent one.
items.plain: We're targeting a new demographic, or more accurately, expanding into an adjacent one.
items.note: A subtle way to self-correct or clarify a word choice. Very natural.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a more precise or understandable explanation of something.
items.example: To clarify, the new policy applies to all full-time employees.
items.plain: The new policy applies to all full-time employees.
items.note: Often used when you sense confusion or want to be very exact. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to quickly apologize for a mistake and then state the correct information.
items.example: Apologies, I meant to say 'increase', not 'decrease' in that context.
items.plain: I meant to say 'increase', not 'decrease' in that context.
items.note: A concise and polite way to correct a verbal error. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to express regret for a mistake or misunderstanding.
items.example: My apologies, I seem to have misread that figure on the slide.
items.plain: I am sorry, I seem to have misread that figure on the slide.
items.note: A polite and formal way to apologize. Can be used for minor errors.

items.meaning: Used to admit that you said something incorrectly or unintentionally.
items.example: I misspoke earlier; the project launch is in Q3, not Q2.
items.plain: I said something incorrectly earlier; the project launch is in Q3, not Q2.
items.note: A direct and professional way to acknowledge a verbal error. Common.

items.meaning: Used to correct a previous statement by providing the accurate or intended wording.
items.example: What I should have said was that the budget is flexible, not unlimited.
items.plain: The budget is flexible, not unlimited.
items.note: Similar to 'What I meant to say was', but implies a more significant correction.

items.text: Let me put that another way
items.form: Let me put that another way
items.meaning: Used to rephrase something you've said, often to make it clearer or more understandable.
items.example: That explanation was a bit convoluted; let me put that another way.
items.plain: That explanation was a bit convoluted; I will explain it differently.
items.note: Useful when you realize your initial explanation wasn't clear enough. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a more exact or accurate piece of information.
items.example: The growth was substantial; to be more precise, it was 15% year-on-year.
items.plain: The growth was substantial; it was exactly 15% year-on-year.
items.note: Adds accuracy and detail to a statement. Professional and clear.

items.meaning: Used to smoothly transition to a new topic or area of discussion.
items.example: Now, turning our attention to the financial projections for next year.
items.plain: Now, let's look at the financial projections for next year.
items.note: A slightly more formal way to change topics than 'Let's move on to'.

items.text: The next point I want to make
items.form: The next point I want to make
items.meaning: Used to clearly introduce the subsequent idea or argument in your presentation.
items.example: The next point I want to make concerns our market expansion strategy.
items.plain: My next idea is about our market expansion strategy.
items.note: A straightforward way to signpost the structure of your talk. Clear.

items.meaning: Used to introduce one side of an argument or a particular perspective.
items.example: On the one hand, the new system offers great efficiency gains.
items.plain: The new system offers great efficiency gains.
items.note: Always followed by 'on the other hand' to present a contrasting view.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a contrasting or opposing point of view or aspect.
items.example: On the one hand, it's costly; on the other hand, it offers long-term savings.
items.plain: It's costly, but it offers long-term savings.
items.note: Used with 'on the one hand' to present balanced arguments. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to provide a brief summary of the main points at the end of a discussion.
items.example: To sum up, we need to prioritize customer feedback and agile development.
items.plain: In summary, we need to prioritize customer feedback and agile development.
items.note: Slightly less formal than 'To summarise', but still professional.

items.meaning: Used to introduce examples of something previously mentioned.
items.example: We're exploring new technologies, such as AI and machine learning.
items.plain: We're exploring new technologies, for example, AI and machine learning.
items.note: A common and natural way to provide examples. Very versatile.

items.meaning: Used to express strong belief or assurance about a future outcome or fact.
items.example: Given our efforts, I'm confident that we will meet our targets.
items.plain: Given our efforts, I believe strongly that we will meet our targets.
items.note: Conveys a positive and assured tone. Professional and encouraging.

items.meaning: Used to introduce an observation or conclusion based on available evidence, often with a degree of uncertainty.
items.example: From the initial data, it seems that the new feature is well-received.
items.plain: From the initial data, the new feature appears to be well-received.
items.note: A cautious way to present findings, acknowledging they might not be definitive.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a personal viewpoint or belief.
items.example: In my opinion, we should prioritize long-term investment over short-term gains.
items.plain: I believe we should prioritize long-term investment over short-term gains.
items.note: Clearly marks a statement as subjective. Professional and common.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a personal viewpoint, emphasizing it as one way of seeing things.
items.example: From my perspective, the biggest challenge is resource allocation.
items.plain: I believe the biggest challenge is resource allocation.
items.note: Similar to 'In my opinion', but often implies a broader view or experience.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a personal interpretation or understanding of a situation.
items.example: The way I see it, we have two main options moving forward.
items.plain: I believe we have two main options moving forward.
items.note: A natural and common way to express a personal view. Slightly informal.

items.meaning: Used to politely propose an idea or course of action.
items.example: I'd like to suggest that we form a small task force to investigate this further.
items.plain: I propose that we form a small task force to investigate this further.
items.note: A polite and professional way to make a recommendation. Common.

items.meaning: Used to recommend that an idea or option should be given serious thought.
items.example: It's worth considering the environmental impact of our supply chain.
items.plain: We should consider the environmental impact of our supply chain.
items.note: A polite way to introduce an important point for discussion. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to highlight a particular point as being very important.
items.example: I'd like to emphasize the importance of clear communication within the team.
items.plain: I want to highlight the importance of clear communication within the team.
items.note: A formal and direct way to stress a point. Professional.

items.meaning: Used to repeat a point for emphasis or clarity, especially if it's important.
items.example: To reiterate, our primary goal is customer satisfaction.
items.plain: To repeat, our primary goal is customer satisfaction.
items.note: A formal way to repeat something. Often used when a point needs reinforcement.

items.meaning: Used to signal the end of your presentation and introduce your final statement.
items.example: I'd like to conclude by thanking you all for your valuable time.
items.plain: I want to finish by thanking you all for your valuable time.
items.note: A polite and standard closing for a presentation. Very professional.

items.meaning: Used as a polite closing remark to express gratitude to the audience.
items.example: That concludes my presentation; thank you for listening.
items.plain: That concludes my presentation; I appreciate your attention.
items.note: A simple and universally accepted way to end a talk. Polite.

items.meaning: Used to express gratitude to the audience for their focus during your talk.
items.example: I've covered a lot of ground, and I appreciate your attention.
items.plain: I've covered a lot of ground, and I thank you for listening carefully.
items.note: A slightly more formal and appreciative closing than 'Thank you for listening'.

items.text: I hope you found this useful
items.form: I hope you found this useful
items.meaning: Used to express a wish that the audience gained value from your presentation.
items.example: I hope you found this useful for your upcoming project.
items.plain: I hope this was helpful for your upcoming project.
items.note: A polite and common way to end a presentation, inviting positive feedback.

to summarise.note: Checker slip: The key accurately describes the function of the phrase in the given example.
